extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry/creative-writing; readers learning practical criticism and close reading
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and interpreting lyric and short poems, focusing on reader responses, technical features (rhythm, diction, imagery), and how treatment, atmosphere, and originality affect critical judgment. Intended as classroom material for close-reading exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for personal emotion / rapture
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers often expect 'personal emotion' or 'rapture' from poetry; lack of intense personal feeling is grounds for complaint ("Its reflective, conversational manner awakens a quiet mood, rather than a rapture, and since rapture is what I want of poetry, it is lacking to me").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit protocols (e.g. 11.2) show readers demanding a personal connection — imagining lines as if they were their own or a friend's increases effect. The author notes this demand is 'illegitimate' to require of all poetry and warns against confusing intensity of experience with poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid presentation and creation of atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Vivid presentation, visual appeal and 'atmosphere' are commonly expected from some poetry; readers can complain when a poem 'does not pause to create an atmosphere.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While vividness and atmosphere are rightly required for certain poems, the critic warns that prescribing these for all poetry is unreasonable; sometimes poets deliberately avoid such presentation. Expectation of atmosphere can lead to unfair criticism if the poet's aim is different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the subject visible / concrete portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems are evaluated on whether the reader is 'made to see' the person or thing described; criticism arises when the subject is known only 'at second hand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protocols (e.g. 11.22, 11.25, 11.27) show praise when a 'complete understanding' or clear picture of the subject is given, and dismissal when portraits of strangers 'seldom interest' readers. Over-description without warrant is also criticized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, simplicity, and probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Merits include 'sincerity, simplicity, [and] probability' — a restrained, dignified style appropriate to the subject (e.g. elegy) is praised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.4 and similar protocols exemplify praise for restrained, fresh, and sincere style ("restrained and yet dignified, fresh without false emphasis, sincere without gush"). Sincerity that masks convention or sentimentality is criticized as naive or insincere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and suitability of metre and language
rubrics_metrics.description: The metre and choice of language must be suitable to the poem's sense and effect ("perfect suitability of the metre and the language").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers often single out rhythm and sonority as primary movers of impact (12.3, 12.31–12.32). Prosodic irregularity or harsh scansion is a fault (12.51). The metre should help impart the poem's mood rather than jar the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy; avoidance of verbosity and ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'economy' and 'lack of verbosity' or ornamentation appropriate to subject is praised; excessive or 'licentious' verbosity is condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.53 praises economical expression; conversely 12.61 and other protocols criticize 'licentiously verbose' language used for its 'mothy aura' rather than meaning. Economy should match the weight and tone of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality and 'criticism of life'
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem that attains a 'sense of universality' and addresses fundamental facts of existence is judged of major order ("poem is in the best sense a 'criticism of life'").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.53: when a poem avoids trivialities and expresses universal significance with adequate technique, it receives highest praise. Universality is tied to positive subject-matter and effective expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique equal to the task
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's technique must be adequate to give 'completely effective expression' to the experience or idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.53 and similar protocols stress that technique — diction, metre, unity — should rise to the occasion; technique that fails to support the intended effect diminishes the poem's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate diction; avoid 'poetic diction' for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should be fitting and not merely 'poetic diction' deployed to sound literary; over-familiar 'poetic diction' can be counted against a poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity vs. obscurity — justify or resolve obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity is criticized when meaning is elusive without prospect of being revealed ("prolonged and very careful study might reveal its meaning"), and readers expect some discernible meaning within reasonable effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.3 and 11.31 show complaints about vague language and obscure thought; 13.31 criticizes poems not worth reader effort because underlying emotion lacks sufficient value. Obscurity must be defensible by value gained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, ludicrous or bad similes and metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Similes and metaphors must be clear and pertinent; 'bad, vague simile' or 'absurd' metaphors reduce credibility (e.g. objections to 'vaporous vitiate air', 'mantles' wise imaginations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.31, 12.24, 12.4 and others give examples of phrases judged vague, unintelligible or ludicrous. Imagery should illuminate experience — when images are worn-out or poorly handled they become commonplace or unintelligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence and unity of structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should avoid being an 'incoherent medley of unrelated fragments' and should leave an integrated impression of subject and form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.32 and 13.131 criticize poems where stanzas/parts merely repeat the same idea or fail to cohere; unity of movement and development is expected for lasting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish and convincingness of final lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Endings and last stanzas must be convincing and not sink into bathos or feebleness ("Last stanza particularly ludicrous... sinks into bathos").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple protocols (11.4, 11.41, 11.4.1) stress importance of ending well — an unsuitable final phrase or weak last line can overturn previous merits of a poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of pompousness and gratuitous grandiloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: Pompous phrasing used for the sake of poetic form ('A^^ tongues declare' or 'vaporous, vitiate air') is criticized as ridiculous rather than impressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.44 and related comments identify pomposity as an anti-pattern; the critic suggests testing whether grandiose language gains any advantage — if not, it should be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of treatment to subject — subject ≠ automatic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic rejects the assumption that a given subject mandates a particular treatment; the poet's chosen manner must be judged on its own terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns ('subject' automatically defines 'treatment' dies hard) that critics who demand a single proper treatment for a subject risk unfair judgment. Different treatments may be valid if well executed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exploiting stock responses and clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on ready-made or 'stock' experiences/themes in order to trigger familiar reader responses is risky — it can lead to either lazy appreciation or severe rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section discussing stock responses (e.g. 13 introduction) explains how poems that superficially resemble familiar themes invite misreading: emancipated readers project their own responses; less emancipated readers release stock responses instead of close reading. Critics should beware of both over- and under-reading prompted by clichés.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intensity from quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Intensity of emotional experience (e.g. 'rapture') should not be conflated with poetic quality; strong feeling is not automatically good poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes a 'confusion between quality and intensity of experience' and treating intensity as a necessary measure of merit is misguided — some poems aim for restraint or subtlety rather than overt rapture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify use of pathetic fallacy / animism
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributing human qualities (desires, imaginations) to natural objects is acceptable only if there is a good reason or advantage from doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 12.4 lists common objections (a cloud cannot have 'desires', etc.) and responds that such figures of speech are allowable 'if there is any good reason for them happening or advantage gained.' Critics should ask whether the device is warranted by the poem's aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readerly 'swoon' or hypnotic movement is a distinct effect (and may be criticized)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poems whose rhythmic movement hypnotises readers into a pleasant mood (leading them to 'loll at ease' and not analyze) can produce private sentimental 'swoon-reading' rather than critical engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 12.71 and surrounding discussion show that a well-handled hypnotic march of verse can make readers enjoy sound in vacuo; the author questions the value of such swoon-reading compared with closer analytical appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of imagery and setting details (consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagery and setting must be consistent and appropriate — e.g. incongruous elements like 'Noon' producing milk in an evening scene can disturb coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 12.51 and 12.6 point out that similes and specific references should fit the scene; confused or inaccurate images draw justified criticism about care and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of prosaic or inappropriately 'heavy' language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language that reads as prosaic (rather than poetically charged) or unnaturally gloomy ('macabre') may be judged as ill-suited or depressive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 12.52 accuses a poem of being 'prosaic' and 'depressing' due to word choice; critics should note tonal mismatches where diction produces unintended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful choice of vocabulary — worn words need adroit handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly used words lose force unless used with skill; originality of phrase matters to avoid clichés becoming trite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 12.24 warns that 'nearly all the words are so well worn as to have become commonplace unless very adroitly used.' Poets should either avoid over-familiar language or rework it insightfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader's investment vs reward — don't demand undue effort for little return
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem that requires prolonged effort to extract meaning is at fault if the underlying emotion or idea does not justify the labor ("not worth much effort on the part of the reader").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 13.31 and related protocols emphasize the cost-benefit of reading: obscurity or muddle is tolerable only if meaning/emotion of sufficient value emerges; otherwise readers rightly feel cheated.
